entry.title: I tried the $60 cioppino at San Francisco's oldest restaurant
entry.summary:
There’s a good chance you’ve heard of Tadich Grill, given that the restaurant is older than San Francisco itself. It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. That was one year before the city of San Francisco was formally incorporated, and 118 years before the restaurant moved to its current location on California Street in the Financial District. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. It’s not merely the oldest restaurant in San Francisco, but in all of California. An eternal landmark. I only needed to walk through its doors on an early evening this August to understand why.

entry.title: NWSL Players Association Has Concerns About Bay FC’s Treatment Of Players Who Have Taken Maternity Leave
entry.summary: The NWSL Players Association is concerned that Bay FC violated two different sections of the league’s collective bargaining agreement related to parental rights, according to PA Executive Director Meghann Burke. One of the sections is about non-discrimination, and one is about parental leave in the case that it overlaps with an expiring contract. The union is evaluating if there is enough information to file a grievance. On Nov. 13, Bay announced its end-of-season roster updates. Three players who are new mothers—Caprice Dydasco, Abby Dahlkemper, and Emily Menges—were out of contract with the club and would not be re-signed. “On its face, we’re concerned there were three moms under contract with Bay who gave birth and were on maternity leave, and none of them are returning next season,” Burke told Defector. “Right away, that sort of raises an index of suspicion, where you try and understand what’s going on.”

entry.title: A Shooting Slump Spells Celtic Doom
entry.summary:
The Boston Celtics opened the season 11-2 and everything looked green and healthy. Jayson Tatum slid back back into his perpetual "No. 4 in MVP voting" status, newly added Paul George was hooping as if de-aged, and head coach Joe Mazzulla's offensive philosophy looked unimpeachable (despite having often invited impeachment in postseasons past). Put the defense in rotation, find an open three, and the math will carry you to victory. Through those first 13 games, it really was. The Celtics were throwing up 43 threes a game (fifth-most in the league) and making them at 38.5 percent clip (fourth-best in the league). They looked cleaner and sharper than they did in last year's Jaylen Brown-led campaign, an even purer distillation of Mazzulla ball. Maybe that should have prepared fans to confront an even purer dark side of Mazzulla ball, too. Since then, the Celtics have screeched into a four-game skid: hosting the Orlando Magic, then losing on the road to the Denver Nuggets, Sacramento Kings, and Golden State Warriors by 10 points, 4 points, 1 point, and 1 point, respectively. That's cause for alarm given that this team hasn't lost four games in a row since May 2021. Sunday's 88-87 loss to a Warriors team led in scoring by Brandin Podziemski, Gui Santos, and Charles Bassey was particularly gruesome. The Celtics led most of the second half, but still went on to lose the game, despite the Warriors failing to score a point in the final two minutes and 30 seconds of regulation. Tatum was 0-of-7 in the second half, including an attempted game-winner over Draymond Green from the elbow.

entry.title: Max Verstappen Couldn’t Pass Up A Chance To Bully George Russell
entry.summary: While both the Drivers' and Constructors' Championships are done and dusted in the 2026 Formula 1 season—the former thanks to almost-child Kimi Antonelli's majestic season and the latter also thanks to his Mercedes teammate George Russell—there are still important storylines to be sorted out, which now includes the continuation of F1's most compelling psychodrama, featuring Russell and Max Verstappen. Late on Saturday night, Verstappen did what he has done in all but one of the Las Vegas Grand Prix races since it debuted in 2023: He won. Verstappen is now 3-for-4 on the Strip, only losing out in 2024 to, of all people, Russell. That part isn't particularly relevant, but it's a fun quirk to this rivalry that has become heated once more. During free practice on Friday, Verstappen overtook Russell ahead of a push lap, and when Russell tried to take the position back on the inside, the pair collided, essentially ruining that practice lap for both. This infuriated Russell, who said that while "there's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap," a move like Verstappen's can screw over the other driver. He went on to say that Verstappen does this all the time, to a lot of drivers, and that he's had enough of it. "Everybody accepts it and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

entry.title: Brock Purdy Made The Vikings Go Bust
entry.summary: The NFL season presents few things as satisfying as a game that promises to answer questions: Is this team really a contender? Is that guy really an MVP candidate? Does that scheme actually work against good teams? These are a few of the questions that swirled around Sunday night's matchup between the Minnesota Vikings and San Francisco 49ers, who came into the game as two of the NFC's best teams, but left the Niners' 35-10 victory as something else. Success against the Vikings depends on one's ability to deal with pressure, and not the metaphorical kind. Brian Flores's defense blitzes at a historically high rate, and in the process of becoming the league's most fearsome defense has raised some interesting philosophical questions about NFL schemes. Should teams just blitz on every down? If not, why hasn't any team punished the Vikings for doing essentially that? Every blitz is a bet that the defense will reach and disrupt the quarterback before he has time to find an open receiver in the vacated space, and it's one that Flores has been winning more often than not. Every gambler with that kind of success rate has an edge, and Flores's seems to be his understanding that, in the aggregate, there just aren't enough good quarterbacks and functional offenses in the league to punish his aggressiveness. Think about how much bad quarterback play happens every Sunday, and ask yourself why any defensive coordinator should hesitate to turn up the pressure on offenses that already struggle with the basics.
